earlier_scan.source_named: Blood, Henry F. 1966/1968. A Reconstruction of Proto-Mnong (incl. phonology of Mnong dialects). Wycliffe-JAARS. Not found online in readable form.

sources.citation: OLAC combined catalog, 'OLAC resources in and about the Southern Mnong language' (mnn), as of Feb 2025 (the Internet Archive); and the Central Mnong (cmo) page for comparison.
sources.note: mnn page lists no primary texts, lexica or descriptions at all (only Glottolog/Ethnologue/LinguistList pointers). cmo page lists Bequette 2005 'A Phonology of Bunong (Central Mnong) in Cambodia' (SIL, not online), Phillips 1973, Kpor & Phillips 1974 lessons etc. -- all Central.

sources.citation: Butler, Becky A. 2014. Deconstructing the Southeast Asian sesquisyllable: a gestural account. PhD dissertation, Cornell University (ch. 3: Bunong).
sources.note: Explicitly Central Bunong as spoken in Mondulkiri, Cambodia (p.102: 'In this chapter, I report on the Central Bunong dialect as spoken in Cambodia') = Central Mnong cent1992, NOT Southern Mnong. pp.104-106: minor syllables are always unstressed, sesquisyllables are disyllabic iambs (final-syllable prominence); p.104 quotes Phillips 1973 'main stressed syllable' and Vogel & Filippi 2006 (pre-syllable vowel neutralised 'due to lack of stress'). Kin evidence only.

sources.citation: Phillips, Richard L. 1973. Mnong vowel variations with initial stops. Mon-Khmer Studies 4:119-127.
sources.note: Central Mnong only (p.119: 'holds for.. Central Mnong, including Bu Nar, Preh, Dih Bri and Bu Dang dialects'). p.120: 'Mnong stops at the beginning of the main stressed syllable are contrastively fortis or lenis' -- i.e. the main (final) syllable is the stressed one. scanned (tesseract, 300 dpi; image-only SALA scan). Not Southern Mnong.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Mnong language' (read 2026-09-17), incl. dialect lists from Le et al. 2014 and Nguyen Kien Truong & Truong Anh 2009.
sources.note: Consonant/vowel tables (from Butler 2015) only; no stress statement. Lists Mnong Nong, Prang, Dip groups (the Southern Mnong area) and the Viet-M'Nong dictionary covering Bu Noong and Prang.

sources.citation: Gordon, Raymond G. (ed.) 2005. Ethnologue, 15th ed., entry 'Mnong, Southern [mnn]' (the Internet Archive 2007); Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds.) 2014. Ethnologue, 17th ed., 'Mnong, Southern' (the Internet Archive 2014).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Ed.15: 'Dialects: Bunong (Nong, Pnong), Prang (Po Rang).. Ra-Ong, Bu Sre, Bu Dip, and Kuenh are possibly subgroups. Probably the same as Pnong (Phnong) in Cambodia.' Ed.17: 'Mostly Dac Nong and Bin Phuoc provinces, south of Central Mnong [cmo], north of Stieng'. Source of Glottolog's dialect nodes Bunong/Prang under sout2692.

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2000. Proto South Bahnaric: a reconstruction of a Mon-Khmer language of Indo-China. Pacific Linguistics 501. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Generic South Bahnaric: pp.6-7 word template (minor syllable + main syllable); p.40 'minorsyllables are inherently less stable than mainsyllables. This is because they are always unstressed, and can be dropped in speech'. p.5 Mnong 'commonly divided into three dialects: Central, Southern and Eastern'; pp.17-18 review of Blood 1966. No statement specific to Southern Mnong.

sources.citation: Butler, Becky. 2015. Bunong. In M. Jenny & P. Sidwell (eds.), The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages, vol. 1, 719-745. Leiden: Brill.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Best modern description of the closest documented relative (Central Mnong/Bunong, cent1992); its word-structure/prosody section gives the explicit iambic/final-stress statement usable as kin evidence and it discusses the Central/Southern/Eastern division.

sources.citation: Vogel, Sylvain & Jean-Michel Filippi. 2006. Elements de langue phnong. Phnom Penh; and Filippi, Jean-Michel. 2000. Le parler Phnong de Mondulkiri: esquisse phonetique et phonologique. 38 pp.

sources.note: French phonological sketch of Mondulkiri Phnong (Central Mnong); per Butler 2014:104 it states pre-syllable vowels are reduced for lack of stress -- a quotable accent statement for the nearest kin variety.

sources.citation: Nguyen Kien Truong & Truong Anh (eds.). 2009. Tu dien Viet - M'Nong [Vietnamese-Mnong dictionary]. Ha Noi: Nha xuat ban Tu dien Bach khoa. 599 pp.

sources.note: Only modern work known to include Southern-group dialects (Bu Noong, Prang) alongside Preh; Vietnamese dictionaries of minority languages typically carry a phonetic/orthographic introduction (ngu am) that may state trong am (stress).
